Article https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-60848-5 Non-monotonic size-dependent exciton radiative lifetime in CsPbBr3 nanocrystals

Abdullah S. Abbas 1,8,10, Daniel Chabeda2,10, Daniel Weinberg2,3, David T. Limmer 2,3,4, Eran Rabani 2,3,5 & A. Paul Alivisatos1,2,3,6,7,8,9

Lead halide perovskite nanocrystals have attracted intense interest due to their desirable optical properties, diverse structural features, and size-tunable excitonic structure. Here we show that, under ambient conditions, a nonmonotonic trend in radiative lifetime emerges from the interplay of size, lattice symmetry and excitonic structure. Small nanocrystals exhibit long radiative lifetimes due to weakly emissive excitons, but the oscillator strength increases and shortens the lifetime for nanocrystals approaching intermediate conﬁnement. For larger nanocrystals with higher exciton density of states (DOS), the radiative lifetime is lengthened due to depopulation of the bright exciton manifold into thermally accessible dim states. A size-dependent structural symmetry lowering transition from cubic to orthorhombic is observed by XRD and MD simulations, and the non-monotonic radiative lifetime trend emerges only in lower symmetry structures with an increased dim exciton DOS. These ﬁndings shed light on the impact of nanocrystal size and structure on radiative lifetime and pave the way for tailored optical materials in various optical applications.

Colloidal nanocrystals, also known as quantum dots (QDs), have attracted considerable attention due to their straightforward and inexpensive solution-phase synthesis and their wide-range spectral tunability from the quantum conﬁnement effect1,2. Lead halide perovskite nanocrystals, in particular cesium lead bromide (CsPbBr3), have emerged in the past few years as highly desirable and efﬁcient optical materials due to their facile synthesis, narrow emission linewidth, and near-unity photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) owing to their low trap density and tolerance for shallow surface defects3–12. The photoluminescence quantum yield is in part dictated by the radiative lifetime, or the time between generation and radiative recombination of an exciton. Nanocrystals with near-unity PLQY and short radiative lifetimes have possible applications in coherent quantum light emitters13 and solid-state laser cooling14. For

example, to observe laser cooling in solid-state materials, two processes must occur in rapid succession: exciton up-conversion followed by radiative recombination, resulting in anti-Stokes photoluminescence14. A shorter radiative lifetime enhances the likelihood of avoiding non-radiative pathways that induce heating, thereby maximizing the cooling probability. One way to tune the radiative lifetime is through the nanocrystal size15,16. For nanocrystals, three distinct quantum conﬁnement regimes dictated by the Bohr radius—weak, intermediate, and strong—are commonly observed. Each regime exhibits a unique electronic structure and optical properties, inﬂuencing factors such as the radiative lifetime. Notably, CsPbBr3 nanocrystals have a relatively large Bohr diameter (~7 nm), enabling experimental exploration across all three con- ﬁnement regimes3.

Previous work investigating size-dependent lifetimes in CsPbBr3 under low temperature conditions (~4-5 K) revealed an exponential trend, with the radiative lifetime decreasing as the size increased13,15. Under ambient conditions, however, the work of Krieg et al. shows the reverse trend16. It was rationalized that higher lying states become thermally accessible atambient conditions and introduce a delay in the radiative recombination of excitons16. Neither of these studies thoroughly explored the inﬂection point marking the transition from the intermediate to the strong conﬁnement regime. By exploring this inﬂection, size-dependent non-monotonicity was observed with a mechanism that relies on behavior common among intensively studied II-VI (CdSe)17–20 and perovskite semiconducting nanocrystals, signifying potential design criteria for optimal recombination properties. In this work, we explore the effect of nanocrystal size on radiative lifetime under ambient conditions. High-quality CsPbBr3 nanocrystals were synthesized to ensure monoexponential decay behaviors, enabling direct extraction of the radiative lifetime. Unexpectedly, we observe a non-monotonic trend in the radiative lifetime. The smaller nanocrystals within the strong conﬁnement regime and larger nanocrystals approaching weak conﬁnement exhibited long radiative lifetimes, while intermediately conﬁned nanocrystals display the shortest radiative lifetime. A microscopic mechanism was explored by solving the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) to obtain excitons in lead halide perovskite nanocrystals, having obtained electron and hole states from atomistic pseudopotential calculations. Strongly conﬁned nanocrystals exhibit long radiative lifetimes due to their small oscillator strengths. For larger nanocrystals approaching the weak con- ﬁnement regime, atomistic quasiparticle + BSE calculations predict a dense manifold of non-emissive dim excitons that, at room temperature, thermally depopulate the low energy bright triplet excitons. Distinctly, intermediately conﬁned nanocrystals exhibit the shortest radiative lifetime due to the balance of enhanced oscillator strength compared to small nanocrystals and reduced thermal depopulation compared to weakly conﬁned nanocrystals. This observation ﬁnds

support from a previous work where the lengthening of radiative lifetime is attributed to the mixing of S state with higher P state that are symmetry forbidden16. Analysis of the present result in comparison to Krieg et al. is presented in Figure S1. Additionally, we observed a symmetry lowering transition from the cubic to orthorhombic structures21–25 of CsPbBr3 nanocrystal system by both X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.However, the onset of symmetry lowering (2 nm) did not coincide with the nanocrystal sizes where non-monotonicity in the lifetimes was observed (5–6 nm). Thus, we do not directly attribute the non-monotonic lifetimes to this transition. Rather, the nonmonotonicity emerges from the size-dependent excitonic structure and only parametrically depends on the nanocrystal structural symmetry. This study leverages high-quality synthesis and advanced computational capabilities to provide a thorough and systematic insight into the size-dependent radiative lifetime in CsPbBr3 nanocrystals, paving the way to engineer materials with tailored decay rates to meet diverse optical application needs.

In Fig. 4a, the powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the nanocrystals with sizes spanning the three con- ﬁnement regimes are illustrated. The nanocrystals in the strong con- ﬁnement regime exhibit a cubic phase. As the size of the nanocrystals increases, a transition into an orthorhombic phase is observed21–25. A non-monotonic trend in the radiative lifetime is observed as the nanocrystal size increases from the strongly to the intermediately conﬁned regime (Fig. 5a). Uniquely, our atomistic calculations capture this behavior across the size range, showing excellent agreement with experiment for both small and larger perovskite nanocrystals. The lifetime decreases between 2—5 nm, and we rationalize this decrease in radiative lifetime by analyzing the size-dependent oscillator strength of bright states. We ﬁnd an increase in the oscillator strength of the lowest bright state as the nanocrystals size increases, independently of crystal symmetry (Fig. 5c). However, this does not cause the large nanocrystals approaching weak conﬁnement to exhibit a reduced radiative lifetime. Instead, due to the increasing density of states (DOS) in larger nanocrystals, high-lying states exhibiting weak oscillator strength (i.e., dim states) become thermally accessible and lead to a decreased Boltzmann population of the bright triplet manifold of states (Fig. 5b). We underscore that the non-monotonic behavior depends sensitively on the exciton level details and ambient temperature conditions. We ﬁnd that at lower temperatures, our model predicts a monotonically decreasing size-dependence of the radiative lifetimes (Supplementary Fig. S8) because the high-lying dim states become thermally inaccessible, in alignment with previously reported experimental ﬁndings13,15.

The nanocrystal crystal structure inﬂuences the exciton level details. The cubic geometries host degenerate excitons and large bright-dim gaps, while symmetry lowering to the relaxed and orthorhombic structures lifts degeneracies, spreads the excitonic spectrum, and closes the bright-dim gap. In fact, we ﬁnd that the competition between oscillator strength and thermal depopulation only produces non-monotonicity for the low symmetry structures where the brightdim gap is sufﬁciently small to compete with the size-dependent oscillator strength increase. In conclusion, the investigation of the effect of CsPbBr3 nanocrystal size on radiative lifetime at ambient temperature reveals an unexpected non-monotonic trend. Larger and smaller nanocrystals in the weak and strong quantum conﬁnement regimes displayed longer radiative lifetimes, leaving the intermediately conﬁned nanocrystals to exhibit the shortest radiative lifetimes. Interestingly, we observed a structural symmetry-lowering transition from cubic to orthorhombic symmetry that was supported by X-ray diffraction and MD simulations. The structural transition onset occurs for very small cubic nanocrystals with edge lengths around 2 nm and progresses to the lower symmetry orthorhombic phase as nanocrystal size increases. Simulations of excitons with an atomistic pseudopotential + BSE model revealed that large nanocrystals approaching the weak conﬁnement regime showed extended radiative lifetime due to the thermal population at room temperature of high-lying states with weak oscillator strengths. In contrast, the unexpected lengthening of radiative lifetime in smaller nanocrystals within the strong conﬁned regime was attributed to a signiﬁcant reduction in oscillator strength, leaving the intermediately conﬁned nanocrystals to exhibit the shortest radiative lifetimes. The observed non-monotonic radiative behavior emerges in orthorhombic and relaxed nanocrystals of lowered structural symmetry due to exciton level splitting that reduces the energy gap from the bright to dim states (bright-dim gap) and increases the density of the lower energy dim states; cubic nanocrystals are not predicted to show nonmonotonic radiative lifetimes. This optoelectronic behavior lends additional support to the XRD measurements and MD simulations, all suggesting that larger perovskite nanocrystals adopt lower symmetry structures. This study emphasizes the intricate and unique interplay between the CsPbBr3 nanocrystal size and radiative lifetime, paving the way to improve and engineer optical materials with desirable radiative lifetimes for diverse optical applications.

Methods Chemicals Lead (II) acetate trihydrate (PbOAc2•3H2O, 99.999%), oleylamine (OAm, 70%), 1-octadecene (ODE, 90%), and benzoyl bromide (BzBr, 97%) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Cesium carbonate (Cs2CO3, 99.9%, Metal basis) and oleic acid (OA, 90%) were purchased from Thermo Scientiﬁc Chemicals. Other chemicals used include anhydrous toluene (99.8%) and hexane.

Synthesis CsPbBr3 nanocrystals were synthesized following a slightly modiﬁed version of previously published procedures3,37. Brieﬂy, ODE (10 ml), oleic acid (0.6 ml), oleylamine (2 ml), PbOAc2 (0.4 mmol) and Cs2CO3 (0.06 mmol) were loaded in a 50 ml round-bottom ﬂask, degassed, and heated at 120 oC for 1 hr. Then, under nitrogen, the temperature was raised to 140 oC for 15 min followed by degassing at 120 oC for 10 min. The injection temperature was then set at 200 oC, under nitrogen, and BzBr (1.7 mmol) solution was injected swiftly. CsPbBr3 nanocrystals formed almost instantly but were allowed to grow for 30–40 sec before quenching in an ice-water bath. The nanocrystals were cleaned in an inert environment via successive precipitation at 10 k rpm without antisolvents and dissolution using toluene. Nanocrystals were stored in 5 ml toluene.

Optical spectroscopy Absorption spectra were collected using a Shimadzu UV-3600 spectrophotometer. Photoluminescence spectra were acquired on a Horiba Jobin Yvon Fluorolog-3 spectrophotometer equipped with a Synapse

OE-CCD detector. Time-resolved photoluminescence was collected on a Picoquant Fluotime 300 equipped with PMA 175 and an LDH-P-C-405 diode laser with an excitation wavelength of 408 nm. Absolute quantum yield measurements were collected using an integrating sphere coupled with an Ocean Optics QE Pro spectrometer and a 415-nm ﬁbercoupled LED excitation source (M415F3, Thorlabs, 14.4 mW).

XRD X-ray diffraction patterns were obtained using a Rigaku benchtop X-ray diffractometer that is equipped with HyPix-400 MF 2D hybrid pixel array detector (HPAD) and a Cu Kα X-ray source (1.54059 Å) operating at 40 kV and 15 mA.

TEM TEM and HRTEM images were acquired on an FEI Tecnai T20 S-TWIN TEM operating at 200 kV with a LaB6 ﬁlament and equipped with a Gatan Rio 16IS camera with 4 k resolution.

Computational methods Molecular dynamics simulations as implemented in LAMMPS were performed on CsPbBr3 and CsPbI3 nanocubes with edge lengths of 2–6 nm using a Lennard-Jones plus Coulomb force ﬁeld obtained from Bischak et al.32,33. Force ﬁeld parameters are provided in the Supplementary Information. Simulations were run in the NVT ensemble using a Langevin thermostat with a damping constant of 100 fs. From an initial temperature of 1 K, the systems were brought up to 300 K by increasing the thermostat temperature by 1 K every 100 fs. Dynamics were evolved for 1 ns of equilibration and 1 ns of subsequent dynamics at 300 K with a 1 fs timestep. The structural symmetry at 300 K was obtained by sampling conﬁgurations every 1 ps and averaging the anisotropy order parameter of each sampled conﬁguration according to Eqs. 5 and 6. Structural symmetries at 0 K were computed on relaxed geometries by conjugate gradient minimization of the forces (Supplementary ﬁg. 6). Electronic excited states were computed in an atomistic quasiparticle plus Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) approach. Electron and hole quasiparticle states were computed within the atomistic semiempirical pseudopotential framework34. Local, non-local, and spinorbit terms were included in the pseudopotential, which was ﬁtted to reproduce bandstructures of bulk CsPbI3 at the DFT + GW level. Quasiparticle states are two-component spinors represented on a real space grid with 0.5 Bohr grid spacing in all dimensions. The ﬁlter diagonalization technique was utilized to obtain up to 300 singleparticle eigenstates near the band edge. Correlated exciton states were obtained by solving the BSE within the static screening approximation for an electron hole basis of more than 4000 pair states. Massively parallel implementations of ﬁlter diagonalization and real-space BSE were developed to enable all-atom simulation of excitons in perovskite nanocrystals ranging from 2–7 nm, up to 7400+ atoms. The source code with example inputs is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ dchabeda/FilterBSE.

Abstrak This study aims to systematically analyze the crucial role of integrating Strategic Management Accounting with Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in enhancing financial analysis capabilities and the effectiveness of strategic decision-making. Using the Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach, this study synthesizes the findings of 29 relevant scientific articles indexed in the Scopus database from 2014 to 2024, identified through the keywords "strategic management accounting, big data, and artificial intelligence." The results of the analysis demonstrate that this integration fundamentally transforms financial analysis, making it more predictive, accurate, and real-time, while also accelerating and improving the quality of datadriven decision-making. Moreover, these findings reveal a shift in the role of accountants from operational functions to strategic advisors, necessitating proficiency in analytical skills and technological literacy. It can be concluded that the synergy between strategic management accounting, Big Data, and AI serves as a key driver of competitive advantage. However, its success is highly dependent on the organization's ability to address challenges such as skills gaps, ethical risks, and the critical importance of implementing robust information technology governance as an essential mediating factor. Kata kunci: Strategic Management Accounting, Big Data, Artificial Intelligence, Financial Analysis, Decision Making, IT Governance INTRODUCTION

The contemporary business world is faced with a rapidly changing environment, characterized by increasingly fierce competition, globalization, and massive technological disruption (Nguyen & Tran, 2024; Andriushchenko et al., 2019; Manrique Plácido et al., 2025). Rapid advances in Information and Communication Technology (ICT), particularly in the realm of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (AI), have become key drivers of digital transformation across various industrial sectors (Sánchez Toledano et al., 2024; Almaqtari, 2024; Pantea et al., 2024). This phenomenon, often referred to as the Industry 4.0 era, compels companies to continually adapt and innovate to maintain their competitive advantage and ensure business sustainability (Andriushchenko et al., 2019; Gu & Zhou, 2023). In this context, the ability to make rapid, precise, and data-driven strategic decisions is a crucial factor for organizational success (Fernández-Revuelta Pérez & Romero Blasco, 2022; Abdullah et al., 2022).

This paradigm shift places significant pressure on accounting and finance functions. Traditional management accounting models, which tend to focus on internal, historical, and aggregated data, are often considered inadequate for addressing the challenges of the modern business environment (Wang & Dai, 2025; Ren, 2022). The limitations in handling vast data volumes, the speed of market changes, and the complexity of inter-variable relationships make it difficult for conventional methods to provide relevant and timely information to decision-makers (Theodorakopoulos et al., 2024; Ren, 2022). Consequently, there is an urgent need for companies to transform their financial functions, shifting from mere transaction recording to becoming proactive strategic partners (Bian & Bian, 2022).

To address these challenges, two main concepts have emerged as pillars of transformation: Strategic Management Accounting and Big Data and AI technologies. Strategic management accounting represents a modern approach that looks not only inward (internal) but also outward (external), focusing on delivering information about both the business and its competitors to support the formulation and monitoring of long-term strategies (Nguyen & Tran, 2024). Conversely, Big Data, with its primary characteristics of volume, velocity, and variety (3V), provides an extraordinarily large resource of information that was previously inaccessible or unanalyzable using traditional tools (Theodorakopoulos et al., 2024; Abdullah et al., 2022). Enhanced by AI and machine learning algorithms, Big Data enables process automation, predictive analytics, identification of hidden patterns, and extraction of deep insights from both structured and unstructured data (Manrique Plácido et al., 2025; Liu, 2024; Jia et al., 2022; Samarghandi et al., 2023).

The most transformative impact arises from the integration of Strategic Management Accounting (SMA) frameworks with the analytical capabilities of Big Data and AI (Abdullah et al., 2022; Gu & Zhou, 2023). The application of these technologies can enhance the accuracy of cost estimation, optimize audit processes by analyzing entire data populations, improve the quality of financial reporting, and provide a robust quantitative basis for investment decisions and business strategies (Fernández-Revuelta Pérez & Romero Blasco, 2022; Almaqtari, 2024; Theodorakopoulos et al., 2024; Wang & Dai, 2025). However, this integration is not straightforward. Organizations face significant challenges, such as ensuring data quality and reliability, the need for substantial infrastructure investments, skills gaps among accounting professionals, and critical issues related to ethics, privacy, and data security that necessitate a robust and mature IT Governance framework (Theodorakopoulos et al., 2024; Pantea et al., 2024; Almaqtari, 2024; Agbon, 2024).

The role of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) in transforming business strategies has been a central focus in recent studies. Nguyen & Tran (2024) and Andriushchenko et al. (2019) have highlighted how technological advancements, particularly in Big Data and AI, have driven

digital transformation across various industries. These technologies are viewed as critical enablers for modernizing traditional management accounting practices, facilitating faster and more accurate decision-making (Sánchez Toledano et al., 2024). While much of the existing literature addresses the theoretical framework of Strategic Management Accounting (SMA) and the application of Big Data and AI in accounting, there remains a gap in understanding how these concepts can be effectively integrated to address the challenges faced by modern businesses. The research by Fernández-Revuelta Pérez & Romero Blasco (2022) and Theodorakopoulos et al. This research addresses these gaps by conducting a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) to synthesize and analyze the integration of SMA with Big Data and AI in financial decision-making. The study highlights key benefits such as improved cost estimation, enhanced audit processes, and higher-quality financial reporting, while also focusing on implementation challenges, including infrastructure, data security, and the required skill sets for professionals. The novelty of this research lies in its comprehensive analysis of both the strategic and operational challenges organizations face in adopting these technologies.

Given the complexity and strategic significance of this integration, a deep understanding of the existing research landscape is essential. Therefore, the purpose of this Systematic Literature Review (SLR) is to systematically synthesize and analyze the findings of 29 relevant academic documents. This research specifically aims to identify the key roles and benefits of integrating Strategic Management Accounting with Big Data and AI in financial analysis and decision-making processes; to map challenges, barriers, and critical considerations (including ethics and governance) in the implementation of such integrations; to present a conceptual framework emerging from the literature to understand this phenomenon; and to formulate future research agendas and directions to deepen understanding in this rapidly evolving field. Research Results

A systematic analysis of 29 relevant articles revealed that the integration of Strategic Management Accounting (SMA) with Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) has a central and multifaceted role in improving financial analysis and decision-making. The findings of the reviewed literature can be synthesized into two main interrelated roles, according to the focus of the research title: (1) Improvement of financial analysis capabilities, and (2) Improvement of the quality and transformation of the nature of strategic decision-making. The Role of Integration in Improving Financial Analysis The consistently analyzed literature shows that the synergy between SMA, Big Data, and AI significantly transforms financial analysis capabilities, making them more accurate, predictive, and efficient.

1) Increased Accuracy and Depth of Analysis: The integration of technology

allows accountants to move from sample-based analysis to full-data population analysis, thus drastically increasing accuracy (Almaqtari, 2024). By leveraging machine learning and data mining algorithms, companies can identify patterns, correlations, and anomalies that are invisible through traditional methods (Fernández-Revuelta Pérez & Romero Blasco, 2022). It has proven to be highly effective in a variety of functions, such as more precise cost estimation in complex manufacturing

most significant roles of this integration is the shift from historical (retrospective) analysis to predictive (prospective) analysis (Manrique Plácido et al., 2025; Abdullah et al., 2022). Big Data enables real-time data collection from a variety of sources, including external market data, operational data from sensors (IoT), and even unstructured data from social media (Ren, 2022; Gu & Zhou, 2024). As a result, analysts can dedicate more time to interpreting results and formulating strategies, rather than on repetitive data collection processes (Almaqtari, 2024). Questions: Some literature provides the critical perspective that the role of AI should not be viewed as a perfect "answer-giving machine" (Agbon, 2024). Instead, findings from AI are supposed to trigger a "maieutic" process, in which the output of the intelligent system becomes a spark for deeper discussions, debates, and questions among management teams (Tiitola et al., 2024). In this model, the role of humans, especially management accountants, is transformed into a "translator" or "critic" who evaluates, interprets, and challenges the results of AI analysis. This ensures that the final decision remains based on sound human judgment and a deep understanding of the context, rather than blind adherence to the algorithm's recommendations (Agbon, 2024; Samarghandi et al., 2023; Tiitola et al., 2024). Discussion

The results of the research synthesized from 29 articles conclusively show that the integration of Strategic Management Accounting (SMA) with Big Data and AI has a fundamental dual role: on the one hand as a driver of operational efficiency, and on the other hand as a catalyst for superior strategic capabilities. This discussion will interpret the findings, relate them to a broader theoretical framework, and discuss their implications for the accounting profession and management practice.

Dual Role Synthesis: Operational Efficiency and Strategic Capability

Findings from the literature highlight the existence of a duality of roles that reinforce each other. At the operational level, AI and Big Data function as efficiency agents by automating repetitive transactional tasks (Almaqtari, 2024; Wang & Dai, 2025), reduces manual errors, and speeds up the reporting cycle (Jia et al., 2022). However, these benefits go beyond just cost savings. This automation is the foundation for a second, more strategic role. By freeing human resources from low-value work, companies can empower their professionals to focus on high-value activities: in-depth analysis and strategic decision-making (Almulla et al., 2024).

In its strategic role, this integration transforms SMA from a mere framework into a vibrant and dynamic system. If SMA provides the "what" that needs to be analyzed (e.g., competitor costs, customer lifetime value), then Big Data provides its fuel (abundant raw data) and AI becomes its engine (analytical and predictive capabilities) (Abdullah et al., 2022; Fernández- Revuelta Pérez & Romero Blasco, 2022). It is this synergy that allows companies to not only understand their current position but also predict where the market is moving, providing a significant competitive advantage (Gu & Zhou, 2023).

Implications for the Accounting Profession: Towards a Human-AI Symbiosis

This transformation radically redefined the accounting profession. The results of the study clearly reject the idea that technology will completely replace humans. Instead, what emerges is a human-AI symbiosis model, where success depends on effective collaboration between the two (Samarghandi et al., 2023). The role of the accountant evolved into a "translator" or "curator" of knowledge. They must have the ability to ask AI systems the right questions, interpret often complex and non-transparent outputs, and integrate them with business judgments and strategic contexts that machines do not have.

The theoretical perspectives identified in the research results strongly support this idea. The concept of "maieutic roles" (Tiitola et al., 2024) underscores that the highest value of AI analysis is not the definitive answer, but rather its ability to provoke strategic questions and debates. Similarly, the "critical discourse" framework (Agbon, 2024) emphasizes the need for accountants to actively challenge AI-generated narratives, be aware of the potential biases contained in them, and not passively accept outputs. In this symbiosis, AI handles large-scale computing, while humans handle judgment, ethics, and strategic wisdom. Implementation Challenges as an Obstacle to Strategic Value

The discussion would not be complete without acknowledging that the road to successful integration is fraught with challenges. Findings regarding data quality issues, implementation costs, skills gaps, and ethical risks are not just technical hurdles, but strategic obstacles that can thwart entire initiatives (Theodorakopoulos et al., 2024; Pantea et al., 2024). A sophisticated predictive model will be useless if it's built on bad data. Similarly, powerful analytics tools will be wasted if there is no skilled workforce to use them effectively.

This is where the role of IT Governance becomes very vital, as Almaqtari (2024) strongly demonstrates. IT Governance serves as a framework that bridges the potential of technology and the realization of strategic value. Through good governance, companies can ensure data integrity, manage privacy and security risks, align technology investments with business goals, and proactively plan training programs to address skills gaps. In other words, IT Governance is a practical mechanism for managing ethical and technical risks raised by critical researchers (Agbon, 2024; Tiitola et al., 2024), also to ensure that technology adoption is not only efficient but also responsible and sustainable.

Lead halide perovskite nanocrystals demonstrate efﬁcient up-conversion, although the precise mechanism remains a subject of active research. This study utilizes steady-state and time-resolved spectroscopy methods to unravel the mechanism driving the up-conversion process in CsPbBr3 nanocrystals. Employing above- and below-gap photoluminescence measurements, we extract a distinct phonon mode with an energy of ~7 meV and identify the Pb- Br-Pb bending mode as the phonon involved in the up-conversion process. This result was corroborated by Raman spectroscopy. We conﬁrm an upconversion efﬁciency reaching up to 75%. Transient absorption measurements under conditions of sub-gap excitation also unexpectedly reveal coherent phonons for the subset of nanocrystals undergoing up-conversion. This coherence implies that the up-conversion and subsequent relaxation is accompanied by a synchronized and phased lattice motion. This study reveals that efﬁcient up-conversion in CsPbBr3 nanocrystals is powered by a unique interplay between the soft lattice structure, phonons, and excited states dynamics.

Laser cooling in solid-state semiconductors, ﬁrst proposed by Pringsheim in 1929, has the potential to advance applications from highpower laser temperature control to quantum sensing and computing1–4. Attainment of laser cooling in semiconductors depends on two sequential processes: efﬁcient up-conversion, where phonons, as thermal degree of freedom of the system, annihilate upon subbandgap light absorption to arrive at an excited state population; and anti-Stokes photoluminescence (ASPL), where the emitted photon energy is higher than that of the excitation electron, as illustrated in

Supplementary Fig. 1. Once an electron undergoes up-conversion to arrive at the conduction band edge, competition between radiative and non-radiative decay pathways determines whether net cooling is observed in solid-state semiconductor materials5,6. Radiative emission without generation of a phonon leads to an overall reduction in phonon population, while non-radiative recombination results in phonon generation. Reﬁnements in growth techniques and surface chemical treatments to remove surface recombination sites led to an external quantum efﬁciency (EQE) of 99.5%6. However, the expected net cooling effect remained elusive in bulk materials, in part due to the substantial absorption coefﬁcient and refractive index of bulk semiconductors, which lead to photon re-absorption. The shift in research focus towards nanomaterials is primarily driven by their superior ability to control photon re-absorption and their consistently high quality, which result in high PLQY compared to their optimized bulk and thin ﬁlm counterparts7. Past studies using nanomaterials have reported showing photon up-conversion and even instances of net cooling which await further validation8–12. Nevertheless, these outcomes emphasize the potential within the semiconducting nanomaterials regime to lead to photon up-conversion and achieve net cooling. Among promising semiconducting nanomaterials candidates for up-conversion2, cesium lead tribromide (CsPbBr3) perovskite nanocrystals exhibit substantial up-conversion efﬁciencies2,13,14, as well as a remarkably low trap density and high tolerance for shallow surface defects, which contribute to their near-unity PLQY15–17. On an ensemble and single-particle level, CsPbBr3 nanocrystals can up-convert photons with efﬁciencies up to 75% when the excitation source is detuned below the band gap by 23 meV14. However, this phonon-assisted upconversion process is particularly delicate and complex because more vibrational degrees of freedom create a larger hot thermal population to excite, but these same degrees of freedom tend to abrogate photoluminescence in favor of non-radiative relaxation. Additionally, coherent phonon oscillations have been directly observed in layered perovskites18,19, and a recent report on quasi-two-dimensional perovskites showed that the coherent oscillations are involved in the upconversion process of carriers20. Here, we deploy a combination of steady-state and excited-state measurements to resolve the speciﬁc phonons involved in the efﬁcient up-conversion process within CsPbBr3 nanocrystals, determine upconversion efﬁciency at different detuning energies, and investigate how electron-phonon coupling changes in nanocrystals undergoing up-conversion. Using a tunable laser, we leverage the exponential relationship between the excitation wavelengths and the ratio of laser intensity to ASPL intensity to extract the phonon energy related to the up-conversion process. We identify the Pb-Br-Pb bending mode, with energy ~7 meV21–24, as the phonon involved in up-conversion within CsPbBr3 nanocrystals. In excited-state measurements, the above-gap excitation results in the expected intraband cooling characteristics. However, with below-gap excitation, an unexpected coherent phonon oscillation emerges at early times as exciton-polarons form within the subset of nanocrystals undergoing up-conversion. These coherent lattice vibrations are synchronized to the frequency of the Pb-Br-Pb bending phonon mode, which implies that the up-conversion and subsequent relaxation is accompanied by a synchronized and phased lattice motion. In all, this work provides invaluable insight into how the intricate interplay between the soft lattice structure, phonons, and excited states dynamics contributes to efﬁcient up-conversion in CsPbBr3 nanocrystals.

In conclusion, our study on the intricate dynamics of excited states reveals that the efﬁcient photon up-conversion observed in CsPbBr3 nanocrystals is driven by the Pb-Br-Pb bending phonon mode of the crystal lattices. We also reveal that, under the below-gap excitation condition, coherent phonons unexpectedly emerge at the early times within the subset of nanocrystals undergoing upconversion as polarons form. This result indicates that the upconversion and subsequent relaxation is accompanied by a synchronized and phased lattice motion. This study emphasizes how the intricate and unique interplay between the soft lattice structure, phonons, and excited states dynamics of CsPbBr3 nanocrystals facilitates the up-conversion process. Utilization of different lead-halide compositions with dominantly higher energy phonon modes, such as the Pb-X stretching mode, may improve up-conversion efﬁciency. Achieving a sufﬁciently high up-conversion efﬁciency in semiconducting nanomaterials will set a step towards realizing a net laser cooling experimentally.

Methods Chemicals Lead (II) acetate trihydrate (PbOAc2•3H2O, 99.999%), oleylamine (OAm, 70%), 1-octadecene (ODE, 90%), and benzoyl bromide (BzBr, 97%) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Cesium carbonate (Cs2CO3, 99.9%, Metal basis) and oleic acid (OA, 90%) were purchased from Thermo Scientiﬁc Chemicals. Other chemicals used include anhydrous toluene (99.8%) and hexane.

Synthesis CsPbBr3 nanocrystals were synthesized following a slightly modiﬁed version of previously published procedures13,26. Brieﬂy, ODE (10 ml), oleic acid (0.6 ml), oleylamine (2 ml), PbOAc2 (0.4 mmol) and Cs2CO3 (0.06 mmol) were loaded in a 50 ml round-bottom ﬂask, degassed, and heated at 120 oC for 1 h. Then, under nitrogen, the temperature was raised to 140 oC for 15 min followed by degassing at 120 oC for 10 min. The injection temperature was then set at 200 oC, under nitrogen, and BzBr (1.7 mmol) solution was injected swiftly. CsPbBr3 nanocrystals formed almost instantly but were allowed to grow for 30-40 seconds before quenching in an ice-water bath. The nanocrystals were cleaned in an inert environment via successive precipitation at 10 k rpm

without antisolvents and dissolution using toluene. Nanocrystals were stored in 5 ml toluene.

Optical spectroscopy Absorption spectra were collected using a Shimadzu UV-3600 spectrophotometer. Photoluminescence spectra were acquired on a Horiba Jobin Yvon Fluorolog-3 spectrophotometer equipped with a Synapse OE-CCD detector. Time-resolved photoluminescence as well as subband gap photoexcitation were collected on a Picoquant Fluotime 300 equipped with PMA 175 and an LDH-P-C-405 diode laser with an excitation wavelength of 408 nm and a Solea supercontinuum laser with bandwidth of 3 nm. Absolute quantum yield measurements were collected using an integrating sphere coupled with an Ocean Optics QE Pro spectrometer and a 415-nm ﬁber-coupled LED excitation source (M415F3, Thorlabs, 14.4 mW).

Raman spectroscopy Low-frequency Raman spectra were measured at room temperature using a confocal Raman microsystem in backscattering geometry at GSECARS, Advanced Photon Source, Argonne National Laboratory. The laser excitation source was 946 nm with 50 mW power, in conjunction with a spectrometer (Acton SpectraPro SP-2500, 1200 grooves/mm grating) and a PIXIS100 back-illuminated deep depletion CCD camera. Three-notch ﬁlters were used to suppress the Rayleigh scattering. Detailed acquisition setup can be found elsewhere40. Data were collected within the range of -450 cm-1 to 450 cm-1 with an average exposure of 30 s. The samples remained stable throughout the spectral acquisition process. For post-processing, the background was subtracted by a background ﬁt with 5th-order asymmetric truncated quadratic function.

TEM TEM and HRTEM images were acquired on an FEI Tecnai T20 S-TWIN TEM operating at 200 kV with a LaB6 ﬁlament and equipped with a Gatan Rio 16IS camera with 4 k resolution.
